mcqs.question: During the depolarisation phase of an action potential, which of the following correctly describes the ion movement across the neuronal membrane?

options.A: Na⁺ ions flow out of the neuron
options.B: K⁺ ions flow into the neuron
options.C: Na⁺ ions flow into the neuron
options.D: Cl⁻ ions flow out of the neuron

mcqs.answer: Na⁺ ions flow into the neuron
mcqs.explanation: Depolarisation occurs when voltage‑gated Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ rushes into the cell, making the interior less negative. Option C states this correctly. Option A is the opposite of what happens; K⁺ influx (Option B) contributes to repolarisation, not depolarisation; Cl⁻ movement is not central to the depolarisation phase.

mcqs.question: If voltage‑gated Na⁺ channels close and voltage‑gated K⁺ channels open, what is the most likely change in the membrane potential of the neuron?

options.A: The membrane potential becomes more positive (further depolarisation)
options.B: The membrane potential returns toward the resting level (repolarisation)
options.D: The membrane potential becomes more negative than the resting level (hyperpolarisation)

mcqs.answer: The membrane potential returns toward the resting level (repolarisation)
mcqs.explanation: Closing Na⁺ channels stops the inward Na⁺ current, while opening K⁺ channels allows K⁺ to leave the cell, driving the membrane potential back toward the negative resting value – this is repolarisation. Option B captures this process. Option A describes continued depolarisation, which would require Na⁺ influx. Option C ignores the ion movements, and Option D describes hyperpolarisation, which occurs only after prolonged K⁺ efflux beyond the resting potential.

mcqs.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes the absolute refractory period from the relative refractory period in a neuron?

options.A: During the absolute refractory period a second action potential can be triggered by a stronger stimulus
options.B: During the absolute refractory period Na⁺ channels are inactivated and no stimulus can elicit an action potential, whereas during the relative refractory period some Na⁺ channels have recovered and a stronger stimulus can elicit an action potential
options.C: During the relative refractory period K⁺ channels are closed, preventing repolarisation
options.D: The absolute refractory period lasts longer than the relative refractory period

mcqs.answer: During the absolute refractory period Na⁺ channels are inactivated and no stimulus can elicit an action potential, whereas during the relative refractory period some Na⁺ channels have recovered and a stronger stimulus can elicit an action potential
mcqs.explanation: In the absolute refractory period, voltage‑gated Na⁺ channels are inactivated, making it impossible to generate another action potential regardless of stimulus strength. In the subsequent relative refractory period, some Na⁺ channels have returned to the closed (activatable) state, so a suprathreshold stimulus can produce another action potential, though the threshold is higher. Option B accurately describes this. Option A is false for the absolute period. Option C misstates K⁺ channel status. Option D is incorrect; the relative refractory period follows and is shorter than the absolute period.

mcqs.question: In a myelinated axon, saltatory conduction results in which of the following advantages over continuous conduction in unmyelinated fibers?

options.A: Action potentials are generated continuously along the entire length of the axon
options.B: Action potentials are regenerated only at the nodes of Ranvier, allowing faster propagation
options.C: Myelin decreases membrane resistance, slowing down the signal
options.D: Myelin increases the capacitance of the axonal membrane, reducing speed

mcqs.answer: Action potentials are regenerated only at the nodes of Ranvier, allowing faster propagation
mcqs.explanation: Myelin insulates the axon, preventing ion flow across the membrane except at the nodes of Ranvier where voltage‑gated Na⁺ channels are concentrated. The depolarising current jumps from node to node (saltatory conduction), greatly increasing conduction velocity. Option B correctly states this. Option A describes continuous conduction, not saltatory. Options C and D incorrectly describe the electrical effects of myelin; myelin actually increases membrane resistance and decreases capacitance, both of which speed up conduction.
